claims.claim: A primary key is a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row in a table.
The core rule of a primary key is uniqueness: no two rows in a table may carry the same key value.
Primary key values cannot be empty or missing; a primary key is effectively a uniqueness rule plus a not-null rule.
A table can have at most one primary key.
A primary key may be a single column or a combination of columns; in a composite key, values may repeat within one column but the full combination must be unique.
Many tables use a dedicated ID number column, such as a customer, employee, product, or student ID, as the primary key.
Other tables can reference a table's primary key to define relationships between tables; the mechanics belong to the foreign-keys topic.
Design intuition: a good primary key is stable and does not change when other details about the row change, which is why simple ID numbers are the common pattern.
Relational database theory holds that every table should have a primary key.

positions: Some designs use an existing meaningful column (a natural key) as the primary key
Many designs add a dedicated ID column (a surrogate key) instead
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are legitimate; IBM documents both terms and both patterns. The lesson presents the ID-number pattern as the common, stable choice without declaring either approach wrong.

sourceRecords.title: PostgreSQL Documentation: Constraints (Section 5.5.4, Primary Keys)
sourceRecords.notes: Official documentation (Tier A/B) read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: a primary key constraint indicates that a column or group of columns can be used as a unique identifier for rows in the table; key values must be both unique and not null; primary keys can span more than one column; a table can have at most one primary key; relational database theory dictates that every table should have a primary key; the primary key defines the default target column(s) for foreign keys referencing the table. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Primary and foreign key constraints (SQL Server, Microsoft Learn)
sourceRecords.notes: Official documentation (Tier B) read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: a table typically has a column or combination of columns that contain values that uniquely identify each row, and that column or columns is called the primary key; primary keys guarantee unique data and are frequently defined on an identity column; in a multi-column primary key, values can be duplicated within one column but each combination of values from all the key columns must be unique. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: SQL PRIMARY KEY Constraint (W3Schools SQL Tutorial)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B tutorial read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: the PRIMARY KEY constraint uniquely identifies each record in a database table; it ensures unique values and cannot contain NULL values (a combination of a UNIQUE and a NOT NULL constraint); a table can have only ONE primary key; the key can be a single column or a combination of columns; the primary key is the target for FOREIGN KEY constraints in other tables. Used as a corroborating reference; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is a primary key? (IBM Data Management Guide)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B reputable vendor explainer read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: a primary key is a column or columns in a database table with values that uniquely identify each row or record; often-cited examples include employee ID, product ID, and student ID numbers; primary keys can be referenced by another type of key to define relationships between tables; characteristics include no null values, no duplicate values, natural keys (existing column) versus surrogate keys (added column), and single-column or composite keys. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
